findings.title: v13/v14 still get 'a person's first ticket due' wrong when the wording has a generic plural ('keys', 'IDs', 'ticket numbers', 'list the key', 'which tickets/items/ones', 'what are') and an order word that is not in RANK_WORDS ('next', 'sooner', 'earlier', 'most urgent', 'tightest', 'most overdue', 'before the others')
findings.evidence:
asks_several (line 341) fires on any MANY_WORDS token anywhere in the question, or on which/what followed by a plural. That includes the generic plural people add to a one-item request ('Keys only', 'IDs please', 'Ticket numbers only', 'Please list the ticket key'). RANK_WORDS (line 54) has only superlatives. It lacks 'next', 'sooner', 'earlier', 'urgent', 'overdue', 'tightest', 'pressing', 'before'; the old ORDER_WORDS had several of these. In those cases `several` (line 420) is True, rule 5 drops the earliest plan, and the list, count or single plans pass, so the rule is not skipped.

I checked this on real banks (scripts and results in scratchpad/review2/: gen.py builds real questions with expected answers from each set's documents; probe2.py runs v11 against v13).

1) 14 person_first templates in PM, on-call and VP style (tpl_order.json) on mdtick, mdplan and mdrep: 308 questions. 286 went from 1.0 in v11 to 0.0 in v13. That is all 22 questions of every template but one, which v11 already got wrong. Examples for Daniel Cho (mdtick): v11 answers ENG-42702 (assignee_of [ticket] → due_date → earliest). v13 answers:
- 'ENG-24111, ENG-42702, ENG-991111, ENG-99123' (list) for 'Which of Daniel Cho's issues is due next? IDs please.', 'For my weekly status email: which of Daniel Cho's tickets comes due next? Please list the ticket key.' and 'of Daniel Cho's tickets which ones due next? need the key' (a phone typo for one's);
- '4' (count) for 'Which of Daniel Cho's tickets has the tightest deadline? Ticket numbers only please.' and 'Which of Daniel Cho's tickets is most overdue? I need the IDs for the incident channel.';
- 'pr:policy-engine#167' for 'Which tasks of Daniel Cho's should be done before anything else, going by due date? Just the top one.'

2) One-letter edits of earlier writers' own wordings (tpl_min.json), on 8 banks (mdtick, mdplan, mdrep, mdblind, mdllm, mdfresh, mdtest, mdwords), 57 questions each:
- 'Which Linear ticket assigned to {p} comes due before all the others? Key only.' (retest) and 'Which of {p}'s Linear tickets is most urgent by date? Key only.' (words) score 57/57 right in v13.
- With 'Keys only.' both drop to 0/57, while v11 stays at 57/57.
- 'Of all the tickets assigned to {p}, which one is due next? Can you give me the ticket key?' is 57/57 right; with '...ticket keys?' it is 0/57.
- The phone typo 'which tickets due next for {p}? key pls' gives 13/13 worse.

3) v14 cannot recover. With a simulated form {kind: key, fields: [due_date]}, 78 of 84 mdtick rewordings are still worse: rule 5 runs before rule 6, and field_fits passes the key-kind list plan.

4) compare_two is unaffected: 216 of 216 rewordings that trigger the check are unchanged, because the clue rule leaves no alternative.

Why it matters for the test: rule 2 now fails if a single ordering question gets worse. One writer whose person_first wording has a generic plural and 'next', 'most urgent' or similar would lose roughly 3 to 4 questions per set. The test's roles make such wordings plausible: a PM writes 'please list', an on-call engineer writes 'ticket numbers' or 'IDs', a VP writes 'keys?'.
findings.fix: Before freezing, change the check so a generic plural cannot override a request for one item due first. One option I checked: add the non-superlative order words to RANK_WORDS (next, sooner, earlier, early, soon, urgent, overdue, tightest, pressing, upcoming, asap, before, top, furthest). This covers all 18 harmful person_first templates above and turns off none of the 25 earlier action-item wordings. The cost: the review's in-passing action items ('as soon as you can', 'before my 1:1') return to v11's answer, with no harm. Another option: do not count bare 'keys', 'ids', 'numbers' or 'list' when the question also asks 'which/what … is/has/comes' in the singular. That catches fewer of the cases (I tried a simple version). Rerun development with the review2 templates either way.

verdict.reason:
I could not refute it. I confirmed it in the code and on real banks, with my own scripts and questions in scratchpad/review2/refute_r3/ (gen3.py, probe3.py, tpl.json, q.jsonl).

How the code does it (cie/src/cie/factbank/plans.py):
- `asks_several` returns True as soon as any MANY_WORDS token appears anywhere in the question ("keys", "ids", "numbers", "list"). It does not matter what the plural refers to.
- RANK_WORDS holds only superlatives: first, earliest, soonest, latest and the like. It has no "next", "urgent", "before" or "tightest".
- So in "Which of P's tickets is due next? Ticket IDs please.", `several` is True and check 5 drops every earliest/latest plan. List, count and single plans pass, so the check is not skipped.
- In v14, check 6 runs after check 5. Its `field_fits` passes key-kind list plans, so the form cannot recover the right plan.

What I ran: 11 person_first templates on mdtick, mdwords and mdplan, 20 questions each, with expected answers built from the sets' documents.
- **Earlier writers' own wordings:**
  - "Which Linear ticket assigned to {p} comes due before all the others? Key only." (retest) is right on 20 of 20 in v11 and v13.
  - "Which of {p}'s Linear tickets is most urgent by date? Key only." (words) is also right on 20 of 20 in both.
- **One-letter edits of those two ("Keys only."):** v13 is right on 0 of 20 in each, against 20 of 20 for v11. The answer becomes the list 'ENG-24111, ENG-42702, ENG-991111, ENG-99123' where v11 gives 'ENG-42702'.
- **Other wordings with no rank word** all fall from 20 of 20 to 0 of 20 in v13:
  - "due next? Give the keys."
  - "due next? Ticket IDs please." (v13 answers the count '4')
  - "What is the next ticket {p} has due? Ticket keys please."
  - "which one is due next? Please list the key."
- **v14 with a simulated form** {kind: key, fields: [due_date]}: every one of these is also worse than v12, which matches part 3 of the finding.
- **Controls:**
  - The same wordings with a rank word ("soonest", "first") plus "Ticket IDs/keys please" stay right on 20 of 20.
  - The "Give the key." versions with "next" also stay right on 20 of 20.

Points that limit it but do not refute it:
- **The pre-registration names this harm in general terms:** "phrased in the plural with no rank word. That is rare."
- **None of the 25 earlier person_first wordings triggers it.** 23 of them use a rank word, and the other 2 use the singular "Key only".

Still, "rare" understates it. Plural means any generic request such as "Keys only", "IDs please" or "list the key", and the earlier writers' own wordings are one letter away from it. The development claim that "none of the 154 rewordings gets worse" does not cover these wordings.

Why it matters for the test: rule 2 now fails if a single question that asks for an order scores lower in v13 than v11, or in v14 than v12. A test writer (writer 1, 2, or writer 3 standing in) who writes a person_first wording with a generic plural and an order word like "next", "most urgent" or "before the others" would lose every person_first question of that wording, about 6 to 7 per set here. That flips a deciding rule.

The reviewer's fix is cheap: add the non-superlative order words to RANK_WORDS. I checked that this leaves the check acting on all 25 of 25 earlier action-item wordings, so the action-item gains it was built for are kept.

I modified no repository file and did not touch blind5/.

findings.title: The development evidence for 'no harm' never runs the new check: none of the 154 review rewordings or the 50 earlier ordering wordings trigger asks_several
findings.evidence:
I ran Planner.asks_several and asks_rank over review_probes/cases1.json (138 cases), cases2.json (16) and cases3.json (18). Every person_first and compare_two case in cases1 and cases2 has asks_several False: 0 of 154. earlier_wordings.py also reports 0 of 50 ordering wordings acted on. So the claims at line 84 ('acts on none of the 50') and line 88 ('154 rewordings … none gets worse in v13') hold by construction: the check never runs on them. They are no evidence that the redesign is safe.

Lines 48–49 say harm needs 'a question that asks for one thing first by date, phrased in the plural … That is rare'. Finding 1 shows the plural does not have to describe the asked-for item. 'Keys only', 'IDs please' and 'Please list the ticket key' are enough. And 2 of the earlier writers' own person_first wordings (retest: 'comes due before all the others? Key only.'; words: 'most urgent by date? Key only.') use no rank word, so each is one letter away from harm.
findings.fix: Add rewordings that do trigger asks_several without a rank word to the development probes, for example scratchpad/review2/tpl_order.json and tpl_min.json. Rewrite lines 48–49 and 84–88 to say what those probes show.

verdict.reason:
I tried to refute this and couldn't. The facts hold. I ran Planner.asks_several and asks_rank over review_probes/cases1.json (138) and cases2.json (16). Every person_first and compare_two case has asks_several=False: 0 of 154. cases3 is the 18 action items, and all of those trigger. earlier_wordings.txt already reports 0 of 50 ordering wordings acted on.

In Planner.check, check 5 is gated by `several = self.orders and asks_several(q) and not asks_rank(q)`. plan_lessons_v13 is v11's lessons with that switch on. So v13 must answer all 154 + 50 exactly as v11 does. The claims at lines 84 and 88 ("acts on none of the 50", "154 rewordings … none gets worse in v13") are true, but only by construction. They show the trigger did not fire on those phrasings. They are no test of what happens when it does fire on a question that asks for an order. The 50 earlier wordings were also in view when MANY_WORDS was chosen.

I also checked the harm mode. I re-ran probe.py on mdtick with scratch cases (scratchpad/review2/verify_f4.json):
- The earlier 'words' writer's "Which of Daniel Cho's Linear tickets is most urgent by date? Key only." gives v11=v13=1.0.
- Changing "Key" to "Keys" gives v11 1.0 and v13 0.0. v13 answers with the full list of 4 keys (plan: label → list).
- The same flip on the retest wording ("comes due before all the others? Keys only.") also goes 1.0 to 0.0.
- "tightest deadline? Ticket numbers only please" goes 1.0 to 0.0 (v13 gives a count).
- "is due next? Please list the ticket key" goes 1.0 to 0.0.

The reviewer's larger generated runs agree:
- r_order.jsonl: 286 of the 308 person_first questions the check acts on get worse. The 216 compare_two questions it acts on stay the same, protected because the choice rule leaves no other plan.
- r_min.jsonl: all 228 triggered person_first questions get worse.

So the development section offers no evidence for the 'That is rare' line at 48–49 or for the safety framing at 84–88. Two of the earlier writers' own person_first wordings are one letter away from the harm.

This doesn't change a test number or verdict. The doc lines do not affect scoring. Rule 2 now fails the check if any ordering question scores lower in v13 than v11 (or in v14 than v12), so a test wording that hits this harm mode will be caught. Lines 48–49 already state that the harm mode exists. The problem is how the pre-registration presents the development evidence, not how the test works.

findings.title: The check misses common ways of asking for all of an owner's tickets: 'ticket(s)', "key's", "ID's", 'JIRAs', 'key for each one'. v11 gets these wrong and the check would fix them
findings.fix: Optionally read '(s)' and "'s" plurals (ticket(s), key's, id's), add 'jiras', and read 'each', or list these as known limits. Do this only together with the fix for finding 1, because a wider trigger also widens the harm.

verdict.reason:
The finding's facts check out. In plans.py, raw_words uses re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+"), so "ticket(s)" reads as ticket and s, and "key's" and "ID's" read as key or id plus s. None of these is in MANY_WORDS or MANY_ITEMS. "jiras" is not in MANY_ITEMS, and "each" and "every" are not read at all.

I re-aggregated the reviewer's results (scratchpad/review2/agg_f.py on r_action.jsonl, r_action_miss_forced.jsonl, r_c.jsonl and r_keys_apos_forced.jsonl). The numbers match exactly. On 28 questions each, asks_several is false and v13 equals v11 for "ticket(s)" (0.56), "Ticket key for each one" (0.56), "JIRAs" (0.49) and "key of each" (0.45). On 19 questions, "key's please" scores 0.44. With asks_several forced true, all of these score 1.00 (0.89 for "pull up all of their tickets").

What I could refute, and why it does not matter for the test:
(1) "Common" is not supported. I listed every earlier writer and set wording (scratchpad/review2/list_action_wordings.py): 25 action-item wordings from the first test, retest, words, blind, blind2, and the general, llm, plan and ticket writers 1-3. None uses (s), 's plurals, JIRAs or "each"; all say keys, IDs, list, or "which/what tickets/issues". The failing phrasings are templates the reviewer wrote.
(2) The pre-registration already accepts this class of miss: "If it misses a way of asking for several, the question is answered as v11 answers it." A miss costs only the gain, never a harm, and the test stays fair.
(3) The suggested fix is dangerous. I forced asks_several to true on the 26 person_first questions phrased "which ticket is due next? ID's please" and "Ticket #'s please" (r_pf_apos_forced.jsonl). All 26 got worse, because "next" is not a rank word. Reading 's plurals would make rule 2 fail on exactly these wordings. Reading (s) or "each" has the same risk ("which of P's ticket(s) is due next?"; compare_two with "date for each").
(4) Rule 1's verdict would change only if both pair writers used a missed form. If one writer did, roughly half the action items still gain (about 0.56 to 1.0), and the gain stays above +0.15.

So the gap is a real but low-severity known limit. At most it belongs in the known-limits list; widening the trigger before freezing would raise the risk of harm.

findings.title: Even on an action item, dropping the earliest plan can promote an unrelated single plan (the owner's name)
findings.evidence: mdplan, the action item 'run token-level benchmark (1k requests) and put traces in shared drive', worded "Whoever picked up \"{t}\" in \"{m}\", which tickets do they have? Send me the ID's.": v11 scores 0.5 with ENG-997888 (owner → assignee_of → due_date → earliest). v13 scores 0.0 with 'Ravi Desai' (owner → label → single). It happened twice, as action_owner_issues-071 and -106 in two generated files (r_c.jsonl and r_act2.jsonl). In the larger file it is 1 of 750 action-item questions, almost all of them acted on (282 gains, 467 unchanged). It contradicts the pre-registration's claim that the check can only harm a question asking for one thing first by date, but the effect on rule 1 is negligible.
findings.fix: Add it to the known limits. Or, when rule 5 acts, keep the earliest/latest plans if the survivors include no list or count plan of key kind over the same path.

verdict.reason:
I reproduced this on the clean tree at c1a26f2 with my own probe (review2/f_owner/probe.py), using mdplan with plan_lessons_v11.json and plan_lessons_v13.json. The question was 'Whoever picked up "run token-level benchmark (1k requests) and put traces in shared drive" in "Trace pipeline & token-metrics lab - Cascade AI", which tickets do they have? Send me the ID's.' asks_several is True (through "which tickets") and asks_rank is False.

- **v11** answers ENG-997888 through owner → assignee_of → due_date → earliest (0.756) and scores 0.5.
- **v13** loses that plan to check 5. The next best is owner → label → single, which answers 'Ravi Desai' (0.694) and scores 0.0. The correct list plan (owner → assignee_of → label → list) ranks only 0.256.

**Why it happens:** "ID's" is read as "id" + "s", so the asked-kind lessons return None and check 4 does not drop the person-kind plan. With "IDs" spelled normally, or with the last sentence removed, asked=key and v13 scores 1.0.

So the check can lower the score of a question that asks for several things. That contradicts the pre-registration sentence "When it could do harm: only a question that asks for one thing first by date, phrased in the plural with no rank word."

**How often:** in the reviewer's r_act2.jsonl, 1 of 750 action-item questions got worse (282 better, 467 the same), and that one is this wording.

**Why it does not matter for the test:**
- It needs an unusual wording and the asked kind to be unknown.
- It only removes a part mark (0.5 to 0.0) on an action-item question. That moves the rule 1 mean by at most 0.5/N against gains of +0.5 per fixed question.
- It does not touch rule 2, which covers the other kinds and the compare_two/person_first questions.
- "Every question whose score changed" is already reported, so the case would be visible.

The fix it needs is a documentation one: add it to the known limits and correct the harm claim.

findings.title: order_test always crashes when writing order_report.md: m["changed"] (the changed copy's measurement) is overwritten with the list of changed questions
findings.evidence: order_test starts with m = {..., "changed": measure(changed)} and reads c = m["changed"]["direct"] for rule 6. The new code then does `m["changed"] = [{"id": ..., "v11": ...} for r in rows if ...]`, which replaces that measurement with a list. rep = {**m, ...} and to_markdown(rep, ..., ("training", "training_all", "held_out", "changed")) then runs rep["changed"]["questions"] on a list. This happens on every input, because the value is always a list, even an empty one. I reproduced it with the frozen CLI command (`factbank_multi order --work ... --writers ...`) on scratch copies of the ticket set, using the dev v13/v14 answers (scratchpad/review2/sim). Result: `TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not str` at to_markdown line 933 (`m['questions']`), called from order_test line 904, exit 1. order_report.json is written first, but its "changed" key holds the per-question list, so the changed copy's per-arm results (the inputs to rule 6) are lost. order_report.md is never written, and the last step of run_order.sh prints a traceback instead of the report. Rules 1-7 themselves came out as expected in the JSON: on the ticket set, action items had n=10, asking_for_several=10, v11 0.6 and v13 1.0.
findings.fix: Store the per-question list under a new key, for example m["changed_questions"], and use that key in `extra`. Then run order_test once end to end on scratch copies (as in review2/sim) before freezing.

verdict.reason:
I tried to refute the finding and could not; it is confirmed by reading the code and by running it. In order_test (cie/src/cie/eval/factbank_multi.py), line 842 sets m["changed"] = measure(changed). Line 844 then stores c = m["changed"]["direct"], so rule 6 still uses the real measurement. But line 866, added in c1a26f2 (it is not in 442223b), replaces m["changed"] with a list of per-question dicts. rep = {**m, "rules": rules} copies that list into the report. to_markdown(rep, ..., ("training", "training_all", "held_out", "changed")) then runs m['questions'] on the list at line 933. A list cannot be indexed by a string, even when it is empty, so this fails on every input.

I reproduced it with stubbed measure() calls in scratchpad/review2/crashcheck/check.py. The result was `TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not str` at to_markdown line 933, called from order_test line 904. order_report.json was written and its "changed" key is a list. order_report.md was not written. The `order` command in main() would then fail too, because it reads order_report.md. run_order.sh runs with set -e, so its last step ends on a traceback and no report is printed.

The rule verdicts are still right, because c was taken before the overwrite. What is lost is the changed copy's per-arm results (the inputs to rule 6) in order_report.json, and the markdown report. If this is fixed after the freeze, the frozen scoring code changes after the test, which breaks the protocol. So it must be fixed before freezing. One fix is to store the list under a separate key such as "changed_questions" and use that key in `extra`.

findings.title: Development's evidence that ordering questions are safe never exercises the new check: it acts on 0 of the 154 probes and 0 of the 50 earlier wordings. Plural-phrased first-due questions do lose their right answer
findings.evidence: The committed out1.txt and out2.txt (I re-ran them and got identical output) show `several=False` on all 138 + 16 = 154 ordering rewordings. When the check does not act, v13 equals v11, so "none gets worse in v13" holds by construction. The same goes for "none of the 50 earlier ordering wordings": MANY_WORDS, MANY_ITEMS and RANK_WORDS were written while looking at those wordings, which is the 'harmless only by construction' flaw this document itself names for the first design. I wrote probes for the failure mode the document admits ('plural, no rank word') and ran them on mdtick, with expected answer ENG-42702. 8 of 10 person_first wordings went from v11 1.0 to v13 0.0, answered with the 4-key list or the count '4'. Examples: 'Which of Daniel Cho's tickets is most overdue? Keys only please.', 'Which of Daniel Cho's tickets has the tightest deadline? Ticket IDs only, no prose.', 'Which of Daniel Cho's ticket numbers comes due before the rest?', 'What tickets does Daniel Cho have due next? Just the most urgent one, key please.'. MANY_WORDS is checked before the 'which of' exclusion, so 'Which of X's tickets…' plus 'keys', 'IDs' or 'numbers' counts as several. compare_two was unaffected in 4 of 4 probes, because check 5 is skipped there. Under the new rule 2, a single such person_first wording in the sealed set fails rule 2. The document calls this case 'rare' without evidence, and 'Known limits' does not list it.
findings.fix: In Development, say that the check acts on none of the 154 probes (or the 50 earlier ordering wordings), so 'none gets worse' says nothing about the new design's own failure mode. Add the plural, keys, IDs or numbers person_first case to Known limits, with the probe result (8 of 10 lost on mdtick). Optionally, before freezing, keep MANY_WORDS from overriding the 'which of …' singular reading.

verdict.reason:
I could not refute the finding's factual claims. Two of its wordings go too far.

Confirmed:
(1) The committed out1.txt and out2.txt show several=False on all 154 ordering rewordings (grep: 0 several=True, 138 + 16 several=False). plan_lessons_v13.json differs from v11 only in 'orders': true. So when check 5 does not act, v13 is v11, and "none gets worse" holds by construction. The doc says this result shows the redesign is safe, but it never exercises the new design's own failure mode.
(2) earlier_wordings.txt reports the check acts on 0 of 50 earlier ordering wordings. Those wordings had all been seen, and 12 of 12 writer person_first wordings contain a rank word, so the check is switched off on them anyway.
(3) The failure mode is real. In asks_several, MANY_WORDS is tested before the 'which of'/'one' exclusion. I wrote 13 probes on mdtick (scratchpad/review2/refute_plural/cases.json, out.txt) using the committed probe.py. Seven person_first wordings went from v11 1.0 to v13 0.0. They were answered with the 4-key list, the count '4', or in one case an unrelated CRM id. Examples: 'Which of Daniel Cho's tickets is most overdue? Keys only please.', '...Ticket IDs only, no prose.', 'Which of Daniel Cho's ticket numbers comes due before the rest?', 'Which issue assigned to Daniel Cho has the tightest deadline? Ticket keys only.' The same wordings in the singular ('Key please', 'Give the ID') stayed at 1.0. Two compare_two probes with 'keys'/'IDs' were unharmed, because check 3 runs first.
(4) Rule 2 in order_test fails if even one ordering question scores lower in v13 than v11 (`not oq["worse_v13_than_v11"]`). Each writer's person_first wording is applied to all of that writer's person_first questions (6 of them in the ticket test), so one such wording would fail rule 2.
(5) 'Known limits' does not list this case.

Overstated:
- The doc does name this failure mode ('When it could do harm: ... phrased in the plural with no rank word. That is rare.').
- It already pre-registers reporting 'asking_for_several_without_a_rank' for ordering questions.
- 'Rare' has implicit support even though the doc cites none: 0 of 22 earlier person_first wordings, and 0 of 12 independent writers', use plural keys/IDs/numbers without a rank word.
- 8 of 10 (my run: 7 of 9) is the loss rate on probes built to hit the failure mode, not how often such wordings occur.

Net: a real but modest documentation gap. The Development evidence does not test the new design's own failure mode, and Known limits omits that mode and its measured effect.

Why matters_for_test is false: the main fix (restating the Development evidence and adding a known limit) changes no number and no verdict. Rule 2 already catches this harm, so if a sealed wording triggers it, the resulting fail would be a correct verdict, not an unfair one. The optional code change is a design choice. It would change a result only if a sealed wording happens to be plural with no rank word, and the history above makes that unlikely.

findings.title: 'With the first design, 41 did' is wrong: on the 154 committed probes the first design makes 48 worse
findings.evidence: I re-ran review_probes/probe.py on cases1.json and cases2.json with plans.py from 442223b (the first design), in a copy of src under scratchpad/review2/oldsrc. cases1 gave 41 of 138 worse; these are the review's '41 of 42' person_first wordings without an order word. cases2 gave another 7 of 16 worse: the straight-quoted "first", 'due 1st', 'ASAP', 'due early', 'closer deadline', 'upcoming' and 'top of the queue'. That is 48 of 154, not 41. The 'Development' bullet sets this number directly against the 154.
findings.fix: Write '48 did (41 of the 138 in cases1, 7 of the 16 in cases2)', or limit the comparison to the 138 in cases1.

verdict.reason: I could not refute it. I pulled the first design's src from commit 442223b (git archive) into scratchpad/review2/mine and wrote my own probe, p_old.py. It asks v11 and v13 each committed probe case and scores both with own_score. I checked that the run imported the old plans.py, the one with ORDER_WORDS and asks_order. Results: 41 of the 138 cases in cases1.json got worse under the first design, which matches the original review's ordlens_corr/out1.txt (41 WORSE). Another 7 of the 16 in cases2.json got worse, each going from 1.0 to 0.0: 'due "first"' (straight quotes, so the quote stripping hides the word), 'due 1st', 'needs doing ASAP', 'due early', 'closer deadline', 'upcoming' and 'top of the queue by due date'. That makes 48 of 154 worse, with none better. Line 88 of FACTBANK_ORDER_PREREGISTRATION.md says '154 rewordings ... none gets worse in v13. With the first design, 41 did.' Read against the 154, the 41 is too low; it only holds for the 138 in cases1. The '41 of 42' on line 72 quotes the first review's count on cases1 and is fine as written. The committed out1/out2/out3 show 0 WORSE for the new design, so that half of the sentence is correct. The error only understates how much harm the first design did, in a development note. It changes no test number, verdict, scoring rule or fairness, so it does not matter for the test.

findings.title: Review item 3 states the finding backwards
findings.evidence: The document says: 'Rules 1 and 3 could only fail when v11 scored between 0.85 and 0.9. In that band a gain of +0.15 is impossible.' The review (prefreeze_review.json, the 'Between 0.85 and 0.9…' and 'Rule 1 (and rule 3) is evaluated, and can only come out not met…' findings) said the reverse. In that band the rules could only fail: they were judged but impossible to meet. They could of course fail at any v11 below 0.9. The fix as described ('judged only when v11 scores 0.85 or less') and the code (`measurable = ai["v11"] is not None and ai["v11"] <= ROOM`, with ROOM = 0.85) are correct and agree with the 'What decides' text ('more than 0.85' means not measurable).
findings.fix: Reword it: 'When v11 scored between 0.85 and 0.9, rules 1 and 3 were judged but could not be met (a +0.15 gain is impossible there).'

verdict.reason: I confirmed it, though it is only a wording problem. Line 130 of cie/docs/FACTBANK_ORDER_PREREGISTRATION.md says: "Rules 1 and 3 could only fail when v11 scored between 0.85 and 0.9." In plain English, "X could only fail when Y" means Y is the one case where X can fail, as in "the alarm could only sound when the door was open". Read that way, the sentence says rules 1 and 3 could fail only for v11 in (0.85, 0.9), which is false: under the old ROOM = 0.9 they could fail at any v11 below 0.9. The review findings in prefreeze_review.json say the opposite. "Between 0.85 and 0.9, rule 1 is judged but cannot be met" and "...can only come out 'not met', whenever v11 lands between 0.85 and 0.9" both mean that inside the band the rules could only fail. The intended meaning can be worked out from the next sentence ("In that band a gain of +0.15 is impossible"), which is the best case for refuting. Still, the main sentence taken literally states the restriction the wrong way round, so the defect is real. Nothing else is affected. The fix line ("judged only when v11 scores 0.85 or less"), the 'What decides' text ("more than 0.85" means not measurable), and the code all agree: factbank_multi.py:831 sets ROOM = 0.85, and line 882 has `measurable = ai["v11"] is not None and ai["v11"] <= ROOM`, which gates rules 1 and 3 at lines 886 and 891. So no rule, number or verdict changes.

findings.title: Rule 3 still has the dead band, measured against v12
findings.evidence: Rule 3 tests v14 - v12 >= 0.15 but takes its measurability from v11 (`measurable` is shared). If v12 > 0.85 >= v11 on the action items, rule 3 is judged and cannot be met. If v11 > 0.85 >= v12, rule 3 reads 'not measurable' although it could be judged. The commit message says rules 1 and 3 are 'judged only when a +0.15 gain is possible', which is true for rule 1 only. This is unlikely to matter: in all 19 dev sets, v11 and v12 score the same on every action-item question (dev_v11.json, dev_v12.json). The document also says rule 3 is not a separate confirmation and does not decide.
findings.fix: Either base rule 3's measurability on v12 (v12 <= ROOM) and say so in the document, or add one sentence saying rule 3 deliberately uses v11's condition and accepts this edge case.

verdict.reason:
I could not refute the logic. In cie/src/cie/eval/factbank_multi.py order_test, `measurable = ai["v11"] is not None and ai["v11"] <= ROOM` (ROOM = 0.85) is shared, and rule 3 is `at_least(d(ai["v14"], ai["v12"]), 0.15) if measurable else None`. I ran the module's own at_least and ROOM on made-up scores:
- v11 = 0.8, v12 = 0.9, v14 = 1.0: rule 3 is judged and comes out False, though the most v14 can gain over v12 is 0.1.
- v11 = 0.9, v12 = 0.8, v14 = 1.0: rule 3 reads None ("not measurable"), though a +0.2 gain would meet it.

So the commit message's "rules 1 and 3 judged only when a +0.15 gain is possible" holds for rule 1 only. The pre-registration's review item 3 ("Rules 1 and 3 ... judged only when v11 scores 0.85 or less") describes the code correctly. But the reason it gives (no room for a gain) only fits rule 3 when v11 equals v12 on the action items. Item 4 does say on purpose that both rules use v11's score. Nothing in the document admits this leftover edge case.

Why it does not matter for the test:
- **v11 and v12 never differed on action items in development.** Across all 19 dev sets (dev_v11.json, dev_v12.json; 159 action-item questions), they have the same score and the same chosen plan on every action-item question. v13 and v14 never differ on them either.
- **The form rarely gets a chance to change these answers.** It can only change an action-item answer when the lessons are unsure of the kind, which happened on 5 of 159 (all on mdwords), or when it names a date field. Its fields were 'owner', 'assignee' or 'creator', which pass field_fits for key plans.
- **Rule 3 does not decide the outcome.** The pre-registration says "Rules 1 and 2 decide whether the check works", and rule 3 "is not a separate confirmation".

The edge case would need v11 and v12 to fall on opposite sides of 0.85, and even then only rule 3's non-deciding verdict could change. A one-line note in the document, or basing rule 3 on v12, would close it, but no plausible test number or deciding verdict depends on it.

findings.title: The breakdown of the 33 changed questions does not add up as written ('3 in training')
findings.evidence: Recomputed from dev_v11.json and dev_v13.json over the 19 sets: 33 changed, 0 worse, all action items. That matches the document. They are: mdtick 8, mdtick_w1 8, mdtick_w2 8, the planner miss 4 times (mdplan and its 3 writer folders), mdblind 1, mdtrain 1 and mdtrainv9 3. The listed breakdown (8 + 8 + 8, 'the planner test's one action-item miss', 'one on the blind set', '3 in training') counts distinct questions and gives 29. Training has 4 changed rows: 1 in the first 48 questions and 3 in the 201. v14 against v12 is the same 33. The table values, the claim that v13 gives the same answers as the first design (0 differing answers on every set), the 25 of 25 and 0 of 50 counts from earlier_wordings.py, and '12 of 18 now right, 6 with a rank word' all reproduce. dev_v13.json and dev_v14.json also reproduce exactly when re-run with the current code.
findings.fix: Write 'one question in the training sets (1 row in the first 48, 3 in the 201)' and 'the planner miss, in the set and in each of its three writers' wordings', so the parts add up to 33.

verdict.reason: Confirmed, and it is only a wording problem. I recomputed v11 against v13 from dev_v11.json and dev_v13.json over the 19 sets in dev.py: 33 rows changed, none got worse, and all are action_owner_issues. The same holds for v12 against v14. Running v13 against v13_wordorder and v14 against v14_wordorder gives 0 changed scores and 0 differing answers. Where the changes fall: mdtick 8, mdtick_w1 8, mdtick_w2 8, mdtrain 1 (action_owner_issues-035), mdtrainv9 3 (142, 143, 144), mdblind 1 (028), and question 021 once in each of mdplan, mdplan_w1, mdplan_w2 and mdplan_w3. Lines 110-117 of FACTBANK_ORDER_PREREGISTRATION.md say 33 changed, then split them into 8 + 8 + 8, 'the planner test's one action-item miss', 'one on the blind set' and '3 in training'. Read literally, that adds up to 29. The doc counts the training gains as distinct questions: mdtrain-035 has the same text as mdtrainv9-143, because the 48 questions all appear among the 201. On that basis 3 is right as a count of distinct questions but 4 as a count of rows. The planner miss is counted once, but it changes in 4 rows: mdplan_w1 has the same text as mdplan, and w2 and w3 are rewordings. The planner writer folders appear nowhere in the table, so a reader cannot rebuild 33 from the parts listed. The total of 33 and the 'no question got worse' claim are both correct; only the breakdown mixes counting units. This changes no test number, rule, verdict or the fairness of the blind test.
